LONDON, April 3, 1871.
/ have received the following despatch from
the New YORK HERALD correspondent in
Paris, dated this (Monday) evening. Your
correspondent telegraphs:--


ADVANCE OF THE INSURGENTS.


By four o'clock this morning great prepara-
tons had been made by the Communists for
an advance movement on the government
forces and very soon large force of insur-
gent National Guards commenced passing out
of Paris through the Neuilly gate. In all the
Nationals numbered about fifty thousand men,
who were commanded by Generals Bergeret,
Gustave Flourens and Menotti Garibald


MISUNDERSTANDING


II was understood by the insurgents and
their leaders that the garrison OF Fort Mont
Valerien would not fire upon them. Accord
ingly the Communists marched out boldly, and
by six o'clock all their artillery was well mp
in front.


MONT vALERIEN OPENS FIRE.


General Bergeret's column numbering some
ten thousand men, was in the advance, and
was marching confidently along the road
when suddenly Fort Mont valerien opened
FIRE upon The insurgents. The first round
killed Commandant Henry. General Bergeret
had just got out-of his carriage when the
vehicle was struck by hombshell and
smashed to pieces.


FLIGHT OF THE COMMUNISTS


By this unexpected FIRE tie troops were
thrown into the widest confusion, and scene
Of panic and excitement ensued. The Com
munists had been allowed to advance so. far
that they were within point blank range of
the guns of Fort Mont Valerien, which raked
their line with much effect. In few minutes
the unequal contest told upon the insurgents.
They broke ranks and in the greatest possible
confusion tried to retreat beyond range of the
guns of the fort.


HOPELESS STRUGGLE.


Although not without suffering serious loss,
the main body succeeded in making good its
escape and finding safety by fight into Paris.
General Bergeret, however, with his column
OF 10000 men, was cut off and left alone
The General acted with great courage. He
tried to fight with field artillery against toe
heavy guns of Fort Mont valericn, notwith-
standing he must have seen that success was
was not long before his column was badly
beaten.


BRgGERET CUT OFT.


The main body Of the Communists, AZ
stated before, succeeded la getting into Paris
Bergeret and his men, however, are COM
pletey cut off, They cannot pass Mont
Valerien, az the guns of that fort sweep the
road to Paris in every direction, and any
attempt 10 force a passage would result in a
horrible slaughter


THE LOSSES.


The main body escaped with loss of some
hundreds in killed, but General Bergere, must
have lost large numbers Altogether the loss
was not less than twelve thousand men in
killed, wounded and missing, the latter in
GLIDING the column under General Bergeret.


TREMENDOUS EXCITEMENT IL PARIS.


A Communist force estimated al one hundred
and fifty thousand men are now under arms in
and around Paris. cannot give an adequate
idea of the excitement which now prevails in
Paris. Ii is something tremendous.

Yesterday afternoon young man named
George Williams, aged twenty-five years per

The spittoon struck Williams on the left side of

Attorney, Mr.. Flack, who was present for the

Moorhead and the Mayor seized Drew, just as

This sudden interruption of the hearing
caused the widest excitement. The wife of
| Drew. and mother of the little child, almost
| tainted, and moment after Drew wept like a

while at the side of the mother stood the other,

brother-in-law left the room hurriedly, but did
not return. 1t was feared he would, however,

| physician, was called and dressed The wound,

length and an inch deep.


| Williams did not return to consciousness until


about seven o'clock, three hours after the acci-
dent occurred. He says he is from Baltimore,

will be resumed on Wednesday. The splttoon

friends of the organization in the North are
bemoaning its fate, it must be destroyed

They were in the employ of the Equator Com

After concluding their work for the Equator,
they went quietly to work for themselves, and
in the course of three weeks had taken out from

seven hundred and sixty-sx pounds and from

A fearful accident occurred yesterday ev ening
in the Cincinnati Railroad iron works, which
resulted in shockingly crushing to death a work.
man named VIM. G. Jones. 1t seems Mr.. Jones
was a hooker-up at the muck rolls At the
time the accident occurred bloom weighing
about eight hundred pounds was passing be
tween the rolls. Mr.. Jones, who held the hook,
instead of catching the bloom at the end as it
came out, put the hook under the side, and,
the heavy weight coming suddenly down
upon the implement, threw the man upon
the betting that connects with the roller
near the floor. A moment more and the
moving leather had conducted the victim
into the jaws of death. Feet foremost, he
passed between the end of the roller over which
the belt for running the machinery moved, and
the coupling attached TO the end of the roller
Immediately above. To stop the machinery was
the work of moment, but in that point of time
the man had gone crushing through until all but
the head had been fattened into shapeless
mass. The very food that the man had taken
into his stomach exuded from the mouth, and
death came SO suddenly that the hand caught by
one of the employees did not so much as quiver
from the awful shock.


1t appears that he fell about week ago near
the same place, but escaped with cut about the
head This is the first man that has ever been
killed at the works, though they have had some
hairbreadth escapes Cincinnati Gazette, Satur-

For the old loves love-sake dead and buried,
One last time, one more and no more,
We watched the waves set in, the serried
Spears Of the tide storming the shore
Hardly we saw the high moon hanging,
Heard hardly through the windy night
Far waters ringing, low reefs changing,
Under wan skies and waste white light.
With chafe and change of surges Ginning,
The clashing channels rocked and rang
Large music, wave to wild wave timing,
And all the choral water sang.
Faint lights fell this way, that way foated,
Quick sparks of sea-fire keen like eyes
From the rolled surf that flashed and noted
Shores and faint cliffs and bays and skies.
The ghost of sea that shrank up sighing
At the sands edge, a short sad breath
Trembling to touch the goal, and dying


With weak heart heaved up once in death
The rustling sand and shingle shaken


With light sweet touches and small sound
These could not move us, could not waken
Hearts to look forth, eyes to look round.
Silent we went an hour together,


Under grey skies by waters white.
Our hearts were full Of windy weather,
Clouds and blown stars and broken light.
And streaming storms and straying fires,
Our souls in us were stirred and shifted
BY doubts and dreams and foiled desires.
Across, aslant, scudding sea-mew


Swan, dipped, and dropped, and grazed


the sea;


And one with me could not dream you:
And one with you 1 could not be.
AS the white wing the white waves fringes
Touched and slid over and flashed past
AS pale cloud pale fame tinges


From the moons lowest light and last
AS star feels the sun and falters,


Touched to death by diviner eyes
AS on the old gods untended affairs


The old fire of withered worship dies
(Once only, once the shrine relighted


Sees the last fiery shadow shine,
Last shadow of flame and faith benighted,
Sees falter and futter and fail the shrine.)
So once with fiery breath and flying


Your winged heart touched mine and went,
And the swift spirits kissed, and sighing,
Sundered and smiled and were content.
That only touch, that feeling only,


Enough we found, we found too much;
For the unlit shrine is hardly lonely


AS one the old fire forgets to touch.
Slight as the seas sight of the sea- new,
Slight as the suns sight of the star:
Enough to show one must not deem you
For loves sake other than you are.
Who snares and tames with fear and danger
A bright beast of fiery kin,
Only to mar, only to change her


Sleek supple soul and splendid skin?
Easy with blows to mar and MAIN her,


Easy with bonds to bind and bruise;
What profit, if she yield her tanner


The limbs to mar, the soul to lose?
Best leave or take the perfect creature,


Take all she is or leave completes;
Transmute you will not form or feature,


Change feet for wings or wings for feet.
Strange eyes, new limbs, can no man give her;
Sweet is the sweet thing as it is.
No soul she hath, we see, to outlive her;
Hath she for that no lips to kiss?
So may one read his weird, and reason,


And with vain drugs assuage no pain;
For each man in his loving season


Fools and is fooled of these in vain.
Charms that alay not any longing,


Spells that appease not any grief,
Time brings us all by handfuls, wronging
All hurts with nothing of relief.

The fower-dust and the hower-smell clings;

Your savage stamp and SAVIOR hangs;
The print and perfume of old passion,

Naturally our cOllegians have found in row.
ing their most practical rivalry in physical
education, and the regattas which have for
many years been the closing event of the col
lege year have been the most exciting features
of student life. Yale with her broad harbor
and Harvard with her smooth river
have taken the lead, but there is
no reason why many other colleges
should not-like Brown and Amherst-enter
the lists. With the American, as with the
English crews, success has been One-sided,
Harvard, on this side the water, being the
winner for many successive years, and Oxford
showing a like score in England.


But the contest has now assumed broader
aspect. Instead of two contestants only, all
the colleges are invited to send in their crews,
and to-day we record a success for the newest
entry over the most dreaded opponent. The
quarrel between Yale and Harvard, through
which the former college was unrepreseDted,
was unfortunate, on whichever side the blame
rested. But as the races are now in the hands
of more general committee, such misunder-
standings will probably be avoided in future.


The Amherst boys who have found leisure
to ply the oar while studying and practicing
agriculture, carry off the prize-making time,
indeed, which has only once been beaten in
American college regattas. The inference will
at once be drawn that the open
air with plows and hoes forms a better
gymnasium than a close room with
weights and phleys; and the men who disre-
garded the farmers yesterday morning, in
their calculations of the result, will next year
be more willing to believe that Yale and Har-
ward are not the only colleges to furnish ia
nous crews.

At seven minutes past ten o'clock on the
evening of February Is very severe shock
Of earthquake was experienced at these
islands. With few exceptions the walls Of
all the stone or adobe buildings were injured.
The cottage buildings at Punahoa are damaged
extensively Many persons rushed into the
streets from their beds.


Three distinct motions were felt-first
shaking horizontally, then perpendiculary, and
the finish was distinct wave motion from the
southwest. The violence Of the shock lasted
twenty seconds, the whole fully a minute.


AT Lahaika much damage was done to
buildings. The Seminary buildings suffered
most, the walls being shaken to pieces, though
they did not fall At McKee's plantation
train Of sugar kettles was badly injured.
Other localities did not suffer much.


At Molokai nearly all the stone walls were



down. The road to the Leper Asylum was
destroyed.


On Lanaia the shock was very severe.
Clefts have been opened on different parts Of
the island, the valley being full OF masses of
earth and rocks shaken from the mountain
tops.


On Hawaii but little damage was DONE.
The Ho and Kau districts received slight
shaking. The volcano is very active, but was
evidently innocent of participation in the
earthquake. Parties on two different islands
state that bright light was visible in the
eastern sky. Chunnies on sugar plantations
suffered little. Several shocks have been
experienced since, but they were not severe.
The labor question will soon be settled.
Two companies Of Chinese have landed here
seeking work-one from China and one from
Tahiti

LIE MANS, Jan. acknowledgement to the
New York Telegram. 1.-The Army of the Loire,
the hope of France, has been defeated in
bloody battle within seven miles OF the city.
The report of cannon was-heard in the city all
day. The entire population Of LIE Mans crowded
the housetops and suburbs of the city and all
thoroughfares, and the progress of the fight was
anxiously watched.


Although the people are accustomed to the
roar of cannon, Il ere never was seen such
excitement. At o'clock in the morning the
right wing of the French army, which was on
the east of LIE Mans, weresuddenly attacked by
the vanguard of Prussans which emerged from
the woods on the extreme right Of the Flench.
Upon the alarm being given the advance of
the French infantry wheeled into line of battle,
the artillery pushing forward through inte-vc!s
made in several ranks. The cavalry took posi-
tions upon the right and left wings. more
perfect line Of battle could not have been
formed by the finest army.


The artillery we're well supplied with ammu-
milton and the infantry with one hundred rounds
per man. The supply trains were conveniently
posted, and real bloody work began. The
battlefield was valley. The two armies occu-
pied heights opposite each other. The French
line was semi circular, and extended twelve
miles, overlooking the valley, which was cov-
cred with twelve inches of snow. On the OPP
posite heights the Prusslans held almost SINH
lar position.


Shortly after 0 o'clock the Prussians began
furious cannonade from the woods, near the
extreme left, fanked by an immense force of
cavalry, the wood concealng their position,
when the troops were massed with the evident
intention of turning Chanzy's position. The
artillery fire continued on both sides until the
ammunition of the Prussian artillery was almost
exhausted, when the Prussians became furious
and gave the order for the advance of the In
fantry.


The French advanced with equal rapidity
along the whole line to meet the Germans in a
fair hand to hand musketry fight. The Germans
were cool and collected; the French impetuous
and behaving bravely, but near noon the Mo-
biles began to waver, and the French, no longer
able to hold their position, began to retreat.
Meanwhile the dead and wounded strewed the
ground, and the fields were red with blood. The
carnage was fearful fifteen thousand French
having fallen before 5 o'clock, when the whole
French army was in full retreat
The number of troops engaged on each side
numbered sixty thousand.


General Chanzy is reported sick, but he Ii
still in command, and 1t is expected another
battle will occur tomorrow.

Last night was dark and terrible. 1t was q

at first it attracted little attention. When

The Ninth regiment triumphed over the
continued opposition of Phariseeism and hot
weather in Boston yesterday, and held its
religious services in theatre. They were
not disturbed much by the sanity citizens,
only two of any prominence even exhibiting
curiosity enough to see for themselves how the
diabolcal warriors would carry out their exer-
cises. The sermon by Chaplain Flagg was a
very good one indeed, and the "Gloria" and

with all the impressiveness and solemnity
of the genuine cathedral organ, except

of lie Sabre" and "J'aime les Militaires" were
piped forth from the irreligious cornet and
French horn. Fisk himself took the pulpit
at the close and dscoursed to his congregation,
expressing the most generous regard for
Boston, and apologizing to the Mayor for a
mistake in the orders Of review, by which the
Ninth failed to salute him. No disturbance
whatever occurred, and the regiment left In
the afternoon for home, refreshed and invigo-
rated, and doubtless with profounder religious
fcrvor than they have usually experienced
hitherto.

text:
The following despatch has been received
from our correspondent at the capital of
Hungary


PEsrH, August 23, 1871.
There is fearful misery in Southern Hun
gary, formerly the most fertile grain -produc-
ing country in Europe. In the district of
Banat one-third of the country is under water


CAUSE OF THE CALAMITY.


The bad administration suffered the dams
which were built to prevent the overflow of
the river Temes and it's tributaries to fall into
ruins. These extensive tracts were in former
times waste marshes, and at certain seasons
of the year completely under water. They
were reclaimed and made fruitful grain fields
under the reign of the Empress Maria The
resa.


, DREADFUL DESTRUCTION.


In spite of the recommendations of the coun-
try people the authorities neglected to repair
the dams, that were gradually yielding to the
pressure of water. The swollen rivers have
now flooded the country for miles.


All the wheat crops are gone. and the
houses, granaries and cattle are submerged in
the water.


MORE CALAMITIEs.


In addition to this calamity the country
has been visited with unusual storms during
the present season, The peasantry of the
south of Hungary rely from year to year for
their sustenance entirely upon the wheat and
tobacco crops. But hail storms have destroyed
the garden fruits and vineyards, besides the
grain and tobacco fields. Even the trees have
been entirely stripped Of their leaves.


SHABBY GOVERNMENT.


The excessive severity of the government in
collecting the arrears of taxes has greatly
Increased the misery of the people. The au-
thorities have seized the cattle of the peasants
who have been unable to pay the taxes.
Some villages owe arrears greater than the
value of their whole property. The peasants
are despondent and embittered, but the gov
ernment turns deaf ear to their complaints.


THE SPECTRE OF FAMINE.


All the agriculture, trade and industry in
the south of Hungary are ruined, and famine
is impending.

Unusual excitement prevailed in Hoboken on
Sunday, owing to the escape of eight mad
steers from the slaughter-bouse in Grove street,
Jersey City, which ran furiously along Ferry
street. They suddenly turned into William
street, and entered the large square just as the
large congregation were leaving st. Mary's
Church, near by. The terror of the people
became indescribable. Men, women and children
rushed frantically down the side streets, many
of them falling frequently in their flight. One
of the animals raced towards man crossing
the square, but the latter fortunately tell, and
the steer swept over him without injuring him.
Three of the beasts took different courses, and
one of them was set upon by citizens and
despatched with knives and clubs. Another was
hemmed in at lumber yard and killed with a
carving knife while he was piAned to the
ground. The five steers hurried through Wash
ington street towards Weehawken, spreading
CONSERVATION on all sides. The pedestrians
took refuge behind the fences and trees, while
policemen pursued the animals The latter faced
towards Hoboken again, but by the time they
reached Seventh street they were either ex-
hausted or killed.

less engaged to be married. During the after

text:
Local politics are at a white heat just now.
Between the Tammany misfortunes of alleged
fraud exposures and the riot, the republicans
think they see their way clear to victory,
provided they can harmonic, and they
are straining every nerve to attain that
union in which there is strength. For
this purpose a meeting was held at
Apollo Hall last night, where more
peace and good will was exhibited than
has been the case among city republicans
for many long day. 1t was decided to form
one General Committee from all the struggling
committees throughout the city, and although
each one claims to be the only genuine Simon
Pure republican organization now extant,
strong disposition to concede and compromise
little differences was displayed. Indeed,
there is some probability that the republican
union will be effected unless Tammany comes
down with unusual liberality and scatters dis
sension again.


On the democratic side the disafection
shows no signs of abatement. The Irish
Democratic Union, at a meeting last night at
Masonic Hall, denounced Governor Hoffman
and the militia and approved the action of
Mayor Hall relative to the riot, while it incl
dentally threw bomb into the camp Of
Stephen J. Meany and his cooperating fire.
brands. But the most significant movement of
the season is the organ ization Of German
citizens, who express themselves dissatisfied
with the ruling politicians of the city, and who
propose to form German party, by which
the immense German vote of the city may be
consolidated and directed to their own benefit.
A meeting with this end in view was held on
First avenue last evening, and was very
enthusiastic and jealous 1t was evident that
the Germans mean business, and intend no
longer to fritter away their political power.


Under all these circumstances the republi-
can party Of the city may well feel sanguine.
The promising opportunities which presented
themselves to the democracy are being use
lessly thrown away, and with the disaffection
Of the Irish and German voters the republicans
need only harmony and hearty good will to
bring them to the front again.

text:
On Wednesday morning, February 1, the
Swiss heard that SO, 600 French had crossed the
border during the night. The possibility OF
such an event had been foreseen, but 1t had
been thought more probable that the retreating
force would have been driven into Besancon to
help In the reduction of that place, as Bazaine's
soldiers had been in the case of impregnable
Metz. But now much anxiety was felt as to
whether the French would yield their arms,
whether the Swiss would fire upon them If
they refused, whether the Prussians would
pursue or whether in many ways Switzerland
might not find herself very awkwardly situated.


The arrival of troop of French cavalry on
the following afternoon put an end to all sur
Musings, and explained much that we had before
thought very wonderful. The horses seemed
scarcely able to stand. They were understood
and half famished. Their legs were knotted and
swollen; their tails and names often rotted away;
the long shaggy hair of their ungroomed coats
matted with dirt. The riders were warmly clothed
in large overcoats, and, what seems to be nearly
universal among officers and men of all arms,
the broad-peaked cap. 1t was the general
mounted heavy cavalrymen would have ridden
over the whole two hundred. On inquiry
found these were really old soldiers, and next
day recognized the uniform, often seen in
Paris, of the Gendarmerie, only without the
traditional three-cornered hat. During Friday
and Saturday infantry poured into the town, the
intervals between the arrival of the large bodies
being filed by stragglers in every stage of ex-





with hanging heads, sunken cheeks, and start
ing eyes. Such multitude of famished, weary,
footsore, ragged, and sickly human beings was
surely never gathered together. Those unable
to march came in by train.


Shall l be accused of exaggeration If at
tempt to describe their condition? l have seen
poor in London and beggars in Egypt, but tnever
such wholesale misery as was here. Hundreds
of poor fellows, their uniforms torn to rags,
limped past. The feet and hands of nearly all
were frost-bitten, causing the greatest pain. On
many q face incipient fever had begun its ra-
wages; many would never march again. In all
the shrunk features and crouching gait told of
gnawing hunger, while the deep cough and
hoarse voice bore witness to long nights spent
on snow and frozen ground. Some had tied
bits of wood under their bare feet to protect
them from the stones; others wore
wooden sabots; hundreds had no socks
and when they had they were merely
of thin Gotten; others, who appeared well shod,
would show a soleless or heelless boot, the ex-
posed pal of the foot once frozen, being now
a wound crusted with dirt. For weeks none had
washed or changed their clothes, or removed
their boots. Nothing but hurried march aud
counter march. Their hands were blacker
than any Africans. Some had lost their toes,
the limbs of others were so frozen that every
movement was agony. The men stated that
for three days they had neither food nor fodder
served out to them, and that before that they
often got only one loaf between eight men,

SANTA FE, Feb. 2.-The Ralston eorrespon-
dent of the Daily Post, under date of January
25, gives the following


week since fifteen men left this place to
prospect for gold on the Chirilla Mountains.
News has just been received here from Apache
Pass through the mail driver, that the party
were attacked by Indians. Two of the party
had left for Fort Bowie to obtain assistance,
and before they left two of their number, Robert
schell and Hugh O'Nell, had fallen. There is
intense excitement here. The fear and suspense
regarding the prospecting party are terrible, as
it was composed of our best men.


The mail from Los Limbres to Lameiseilla has
been captured by the Indians. Captain Bowie
left an hour after the news had reached there,
with detachment of twenty-five men, to render
aid. The Indians also stole and drove off about
three thousand sheep belonging to Christebran
Chames. of Bender. Two men were supposed to
have been killed by the Indians, as they have not
been heard from since Monday. Several citizens
started in pursuit, but they have not yet been
heard from. The Indians drove the sheep in
the direction of the White Mountains.

On Saturday night boat containing two

shooting, was caught in the ice opposite the
United States army post at David's Island,
and was rapidly carried towards the open
sound. Lieutenant P. II. Ray, of the 9th
Infantry, stationed on Davids Island, saw the
peril in which the duck hunters were placed,

to their rescue. He succeeded in rescu-
ing the two civilians and in getting them
into his boat, but then discovered that he too,
with his party, was hopelessly caught in the
ice, and that return to the island was impos-
sible. The cold was intense, and although the
men endesvored to keep themselves alive by
beating one another, they were soon be-
numbed into utter helplessness. All night
long fires were burned, muskets discharged,
and bugles sounded on David's Island, and
early yesterday morning Lieutenant Ray and
his party were seen jammed in the Ice above
City Island.


volunteer crew, consistingof Lieutenants
Corlies, Craig, Ernest, and Summerhays, Ser
geant Fernald, and five men, started to their
rescue, and with axes cut their way through
the ice to their nearly frozen comrades.
Much excitement existel on David's Island
when the men, who had been exposed to the
storm sixteen hours, were carried on shore
Every attention was paid them, and although
they are suffering from severe frost bites, they
are all in a fair way to recover.
